articles.title: Sephora API Example: A Price and Stock Check Tool for an AI Agent
articles.description: Ask an AI agent what Rare Beauty's Soft Pinch Liquid Blush costs at Sephora, and the first thing it sees is the search result: "listPrice": "$16.00 - $25.00". Which number goes in the answer? The $16 is a 3.2 mL mini. The $25 is the 7.5 mL full size. Per millilitre, the mini costs 50% more. That is not a rare case. I asked the Sephora API 15 shopping questions, typed the way a shopper types them, and 11 of the 15 products came back with a range instead of a price. Search itself did well: the first result matched the product named in 15 of 15 questions. The trouble starts after that, when the agent has to pick a size, a shade and a store. What I asked, and how The questions were the plain kind: "dior lip glow oil", "tatcha water cream", "ysl libre perfume", "dyson airwrap", "olaplex no 3", and ten more across makeup, skincare, hair and fragrance. For each one I ran what an agent connected to the Sephora API would run, on 4 November 2026: /search-by-keyword with the question, 10 results. /product-details for the product the shopper meant, which lists every size and shade as a SKU. /product-availability for that product's default SKU, within 10 miles of one of five US cities (New York, Chicago, Los Angeles, Houston, Seattle). Over MCP, these are three tools: RapidAPI's gateway turns every endpoint of the API into one (how to connect it). So the raw responses below are exactly what a model would read. In all that was 116 search rows, 15 product records with 140 SKUs, and 204 store rows. The search price is usually a range Product Search says Default SKU Best value Smallest size pays Rare Beauty Soft Pinch Blush $16.00 - $25.00 7.5 mL, $25 7.5 mL, $3.33/mL +50% Drunk Elephant Protini $24.00 - $99.00 50 mL, $72 100 mL, $0.99/mL +62% Glow Recipe Dew Drops $20.00 - $49.00 40 mL, $36 80 mL, $0.61/mL +118% The Ordinary Niacinamide $6.00 - $10.80 30 mL, $6 60 mL, $0.18/mL +11% Sol de Janeiro Bum Bum Cream $24.00 - $48.00 240 mL, $48 240 mL at $44, $0.18/mL +75% Olaplex No.3PLUS $34.00 - $68.00 100 mL, $34 250 mL, $0.27/mL +25% Tatcha The Water Cream $25.00 - $93.00 50 mL, $74 75 mL, $1.24/mL +34% YSL Libre Eau de Parfum $38.00 - $225.00 90 mL, $185 100 mL, $1.40/mL +171% Huda Beauty Easy Bake $24.00 - $42.00 2 x 6.5 g, $42 20 g, $2.00/g +100% In 9 of the 11 ranges, the low end is the price of the smallest size. An agent that reports "from $24" for Drunk Elephant's Protini is quoting a 15 mL jar of a cream most people buy at 50 mL. An agent that reports the high end is often quoting the biggest bottle. Neither is what the shopper meant by "how much is it". The product record does not settle it either. Each product has a default SKU (the currentSku in /product-details, the same SKU the search row points to for 13 of the 15), and it is often neither the cheapest nor the most common size. For YSL Libre it is the 90 mL bottle at $185. For Glow Recipe it is the 40 mL at $36, a size the search range never mentions. Per millilitre or gram, the smallest size cost more in all 9 products with a real choice of sizes, a median of 62% more than the best-value size. YSL Libre is the extreme: the 10 mL spray works out at $3.80/mL, the best value is $1.40/mL. And that best value is not the biggest bottle. The 100 mL at $140 costs less than the 90 mL at $185, and it is the one SKU with isOnlineOnly: true. An agent comparing sizes by eye would miss it. An agent that computes price per mL finds it at once. Shades and models have prices too 11 of the 15 products carried more than one list price across their SKUs. Sizes explain most of it, but not all. Laneige's Lip Sleeping Mask costs $24 in most flavours and $25 in three, two of them limited editions. Charlotte Tilbury's Matte Revolution costs $37, except in two shades at $39. So "how much is the Pillow Talk lipstick" has a right answer only after the agent resolves the shade to a SKU. Dyson is the other kind of ambiguity. The search for "dyson airwrap" returned 7 different multi-stylers in the top 10, at $649, $699 and $749, plus attachments. The first one, the agent's natural pick, had isOutOfStock: true on its only SKU, and none of the 6 stores near Houston had it. A good answer there is a question back to the user: which Airwrap? Store stock: read the units, not the label Across the 204 store rows, 160 said "In Stock", 18 "Limited Stock" and 26 "Out of Stock". 14 of the 15 products were on a shelf somewhere near their city. Three details matter for an agent: The label is not a unit count. 4 store rows said "In Stock" with exactly 1 unit on hand. 4 said "Limited Stock" with 5 or more, up to 21 for The Ordinary's serum in Houston. If the user is about to drive somewhere, inStoreAvailability is the number to pass on. Some stores are inside Kohl's. 24 of the 204 rows were Sephora counters inside Kohl's stores (storeType is not SEPHORA), and 15 of them had the item. That is worth saying in the answer, because a shopper heading to "the Sephora in Jersey City" will not find a standalone store. The search row's pickup flag says nothing about stores. pickupEligible was false on all 116 search rows, including the 14 products that were in stock nearby. It describes the search context, not shelves. Only /product-availability answers "can I pick it up today?" The tool None of this needs a model to reason about it. It needs a tool that does the arithmetic and hands the model a short answer: every size once with its price per mL or gram, the SKU for the shade the user named, and the nearest stores with units. Here is that tool, runnable as printed with a RapidAPI key: """A price and stock check tool for an AI agent, over the Sephora API on RapidAPI. Three calls (search, product record, store stock) in, one small answer out: every size with its price per mL or gram, the shade or size the shopper asked for, and the nearest stores that have it. RAPIDAPI_KEY=... python3 sephora_price_check.py "rare beauty soft pinch liquid blush" Happy 40.758 -73.9855 """ import json import os import re import sys import requests HOST = "real-time-sephora-api.p.rapidapi.com" BASE = os.environ.get("API_BASE", "https://" + HOST) def headers(): if "API_BASE" in os.environ: return json.loads(os.environ.get("API_HEADERS", "{}")) return {"x-rapidapi-host": HOST, "x-rapidapi-key": os.environ["RAPIDAPI_KEY"]} def get(path, **params): r = requests.get(BASE + path, params=params, headers=headers(), timeout=60) return r.json() def dollars(text): m = re.search(r"\$([\d,]+(?:\.\d+)?)", text or "") return float(m.group(1).replace(",", "")) if m else None def amount(size): """'0.25 oz/ 7.5 mL' -> (7.5, 'mL'), '0.21 oz/6 g' -> (6.0, 'g'). None if neither is given.""" m = re.search(r"([\d.]+)\s*ml", size or "", re.I) or re.search(r"([\d.]+)\s*g\b", size or "", re.I) if not m: return None return float(m.group(1)), "mL" if "ml" in m.group(0).lower() else "g" def sku_row(k): price = dollars(k.get("salePrice")) or dollars(k.get("listPrice")) a = amount(k.get("size")) return { "sku": k["skuId"], "option": k.get("variationValue"), "size": (k.get("size") or "").strip() or None, "price_usd": price, "was_usd": dollars(k.get("listPrice")) if k.get("salePrice") else None, "per_unit": "%.2f/%s" % (price / a[0], a[1]) if a and price else None, "online_only": k.get("isOnlineOnly"), "sold_out_online": k.get("isOutOfStock"), } def check_price(query, option=None, lat=None, lon=None): rows = get("/search-by-keyword", keyword=query, pageSize=10) full_size = [r for r in rows if not r["displayName"].lower().startswith("mini ")] if not full_size: return {"error": "no product found for %r" % query} product = full_size[0] details = get("/product-details", productId=product["productId"]) skus, seen = [], set() for k in [details["currentSku"]] + details.get("regularChildSkus", []): if k["skuId"] not in seen: chosen = skus[0] # the product's default SKU if option: chosen = next((s for s in skus if option.lower() in (s["option"] or "").lower()), chosen) # Many shades share a size and a price, spelled several ways: list each size and price once sizes = {} for s in skus: key = (amount(s["size"]) or s["size"], s["price_usd"]) answer = { "product": "%s %s" % (product["brandName"], product["displayName"]), "url": details.get("fullSiteProductUrl"), "chosen": chosen, "sizes": [{"size": v["size"], "price_usd": v["price_usd"], "per_unit": v["per_unit"], "online_only": v["online_only"], "options": v["options"]} for v in sizes.values()], if lat is not None: stock = get("/product-availability", skuId=chosen["sku"], latitude=lat, longitude=lon, radius=10) stores = stock["data"]["stores"] answer["stores"] = [{"store": x["displayName"], "miles": x["distance"], "units": x["inStoreAvailability"], "status": x["availabilityStatus"], "inside_kohls": x["storeType"] != "SEPHORA"} for x in stores if x["inStoreAvailability"] > 0][:5] answer["stores_checked"] = len(stores) return answer if __name__ == "__main__": q = sys.argv[1] opt = sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else None lat, lon = (float(sys.argv[3]), float(sys.argv[4])) if len(sys.argv) > 4 else (None, None) result = check_price(q, opt, lat, lon) print(json.dumps(result, indent=1)) print("answer: %d characters" % len(json.dumps(result, separators=(",", ":")))) For the blush in the shade Happy, near Times Square, it chose SKU 2362085 (7.5 mL, $25, $3.33/mL), listed the two sizes once each (14 shades of the full size, 8 of the mini at $5.00/mL), and returned the five nearest stores with units, Times Square first with 97. The whole answer was 1,007 characters. The three raw responses behind it run to about 199,000 characters in my test calls (13,228 for the search, 129,780 for the product record, about 55,700 for the stores), roughly 49,700 tokens at four characters a token. That is an estimate, since every model's tokenizer differs, but the gap is the point. To give it to Claude or another agent, wrap check_price as one tool with three inputs (query, option, and a location), in whatever framework you use, or as a tool of your own MCP server next to the gateway's endpoint tools. Pitfalls in the data Size strings are free text. Fenty's Gloss Bomb has 10 SKUs and 7 spellings of its size, among them 0.3 oz/ 9 mL, 0.30 oz, 0.3 oz/9 oz and 0.30 oz/9 g. Huda Beauty's powder has 7. Parse the mL or gram figure, and treat a size with neither as unknown. Four SKUs had no size at all. Same size, different price. Sol de Janeiro's Bum Bum Cream has two 240 mL SKUs, at $48 and $44, and nothing in the size field says how they differ. Tatcha and Drunk Elephant list refills of the 50 mL at $68 and $63 next to the jars at $74 and $72; there the size says "Refill". Show the user both. Minis live in two places. A mini is often both a SKU of the main product and a separate "Mini ..." product in search. 39 of the 116 search rows were minis or sets. The tool skips the "Mini" products in search and gets the mini sizes from the main record, so each size appears once. Sales are rare and live in salePrice. Only 1 of the 116 search rows was on sale (a Charlotte Tilbury mini lipstick set, $26 down to $18.20). When salePrice is set, it is the price, and listPrice is the was-price. The range and the record can disagree. For 14 of the 15 products, the search range matched the lowest and highest SKU prices exactly. For Laneige's mask, the range started at $23 while every SKU in the product record cost $24 or $25. Quote the record. What I would do next Add a size preference to the tool ("the usual size", "the best value", "travel size") so the agent can answer the question the user asked without asking back, and cache product records for a day, since prices change less often than stock. The Sephora API is on RapidAPI with a free plan for testing. More examples are in the Sephora API repo on GitHub, and the Sephora API overview on LinkedIn covers what the data includes. articles.title: SIMPLE law predicts quadratic prefill cost
articles.description: "prefill energy grows quadratically with the hidden dimension, so larger LLMs suffer most from long inputs;" [1]. That closed‑form observation collapses years of ad‑hoc profiling into a single analytic curve. It simultaneously predicts how much extra work each new token imposes on the KV‑cache and where the sweet spot between prompt length and compute lies. In practice, engineers can now plug model size and desired context into one equation and obtain a realistic energy budget. Before this work, inference cost estimators were essentially black‑box fits that required a separate calibration for every architecture. State‑of‑the‑art models swallowed architectural hyperparameters into dozens of coefficients, sacrificing interpretability for marginal accuracy. As a result, scaling studies had to rerun expensive traces whenever a new model variant appeared. The field lacked a principled way to separate the cost of loading an input from the incremental cost of generating each token. "The Prefill Amortization term grows quadratically with , while the Decode Accumulation terms grow only linearly: the KV‑cache term is proportional to , and the Next-token term is affine in due to the constant offset ." [1]. This decomposition shows that the dominant driver of early‑stage compute is a quadratic function of hidden size, whereas the per‑step decode overhead scales linearly with the number of cached keys and values. Consequently, doubling the hidden dimension quadruples the prefill energy, but adding another thousand tokens only adds a linear increment. The formula makes the trade‑off explicit: larger models demand shorter prompts if energy consumption is to stay bounded. KV‑cache energy is proportional to context length, contributing to the super‑linear growth observed when reasoning token budgets expand, together with the quadratic prefill term. As more tokens are generated, each new key‑value pair must be read and written for every subsequent step, inflating the memory‑access cost faster than the pure compute term. This explains why extending a reasoning window beyond an analytically derived optimum hurts “intelligence per joule” by up to threefold across a four‑fold budget increase. The linear KV term therefore becomes the bottleneck in long‑generation scenarios. "with only four parameters fitted once across all LLMs, it reduces the error of previous SOTA models by 3.1–3.5, reaching a MAPE of 11.97%." [1]. Across traces of thirteen dense models on H100 GPUs the SIMPLE law attains an R² of 0.969, confirming that the compact formula captures real hardware behavior. Its prediction error is three to three‑and‑a‑half times lower than earlier empirical fits, despite using a single parameter set for every architecture. The result validates that a tiny analytical model can replace heavyweight per‑model calibration. The study leaves open how well the law transfers to sparsely activated transformers, quantized weights, or non‑NVIDIA accelerators. Its derivation assumes dense matrix multiplications and ignores cache‑hierarchy effects that may dominate on CPUs or edge GPUs. Moreover, while energy is a critical proxy for cost, latency and throughput are not directly addressed; a model could be energy‑efficient yet too slow for real‑time serving. These gaps suggest a research agenda around extending the SIMPLE framework to heterogeneous hardware and richer performance metrics. If engineers adopt the quadratic‑prefill insight as a first‑order budget check, they can prune prompts before running any inference, saving both time and electricity. Benchmarks that sweep context length should now report the SIMPLE‑predicted energy curve alongside empirical latency, allowing a direct comparison of theoretical minima versus observed sweet spots. By treating the four‑parameter law as a design constraint, product teams can decide whether to invest in longer KV caches, more aggressive GQA grouping, or simply smaller hidden dimensions for cost‑sensitive deployments. Will future KV‑cache architectures rewrite this quadratic rule, or will engineers simply learn to live within its limits? References The SIMPLE Law for Energy Cost of LLM Inference

articles.title: GitHub-hosted vs self-hosted vs managed runners
articles.description: The github hosted vs self hosted runners question has a third answer that did not exist when the question was first asked, and for most teams it is the right one: managed runners. Stay GitHub-hosted while your minutes fit the included allowance or your repositories are public, go self-hosted when you need hardware, network position or persistent state that nobody rents, and take managed runners for everything in between, which is most CI. The same job under three models, with the published rates read 20 September 2026. The self-hosted column has no per-minute rate because GitHub charges nothing for it. Every GitHub Actions job runs on a runner, and there are exactly three places that runner can come from: GitHub, you, or a vendor who operates it for you. That choice is the largest single lever on what CI costs and how much of your week it takes. They are not a ladder you climb but three trades: GitHub-hosted trades money for zero setup, self-hosted trades your time for control, and managed runners trade a vendor relationship for most of the self-hosted economics without the pager. Plenty of mature teams run all three at once, because runner selection is per job. Every rate and limit below was read from docs.github.com or the named vendor's own page on 20 September 2026, and GitHub's included allowance, now a dollar amount, was read again on 12 November 2026. The self-hosted column has no published per-minute rate, and says so rather than carrying a made-up figure. Comparison GitHub-hosted Self-hosted Managed (Latchkey shown) Price per minute, 2 vCPU Linux x64 $0.006 on a private repo (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 14 GB SSD); free and unlimited on public repos Not published, because GitHub does not charge for it: its billing page states Actions usage is free for self-hosted runners. You pay your cloud bill, including the idle minutes between jobs $0.0025 (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 100 GB disk) Price per minute, 4 vCPU Linux x64 $0.012 as a larger runner; the free public-repo standard runner is already 4 vCPU and 16 GB Your instance rate. A 4 vCPU cloud VM is cheap per hour and expensive per idle hour, which is the whole economic argument $0.005 (4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 100 GB disk) Free tier $12 of included compute a month on Free, $18 on Team, $300 on Enterprise Cloud (2,000, 3,000 and 50,000 standard Linux minutes at $0.006), private repos only; on Team and Enterprise Cloud larger runners can draw on it, and they are billed on public repos Unlimited from GitHub. Your cloud provider has opinions 30-day trial, then 2,000 included minutes a month on Developer, 4,000 on Launch, 6,000 on Scale Billing granularity Every job is rounded up to the nearest whole minute Your cloud provider's, which is usually per second with a minimum, applied to instance uptime rather than job time Per minute Runner sizes and OS Linux x64 and arm64, Windows x64 and arm64, macOS on M-series and Intel; larger runners to 96 vCPU x64 and 64 vCPU arm64 Anything you can boot and install the runner agent on, including hardware nobody rents: GPUs, bare metal, an on-premises box next to the license dongle Varies by vendor. Latchkey is 2 to 16 vCPU on Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64 only; Blacksmith and Depot add arm64, Windows and macOS Cache: type, limit, persistence actions/cache, 10 GB per repository, entries removed after 7 days without access, restorable only from the same or the default branch actions/cache still goes to GitHub and keeps the same 10 GB limit, unless you run your own cache server. What you do get free is a warm local disk between jobs Vendor-provided and usually larger: Latchkey publishes no size and keeps entries 14 days, 25 GB per repo per week on Blacksmith, metered storage on Depot and Namespace Docker build acceleration None built in. cache-to: type=gha writes into the same 10 GB store Whatever you build. A persistent BuildKit cache on a long-lived host is the single best reason to self-host, and it is also the thing that fills the disk Vendor actions with a managed layer cache: latchkey-dev/docker-cache-action@v1, or Blacksmith's builder on a sticky disk Concurrency limits 20 concurrent jobs on Free, 40 on Pro, 60 on Team, 500 on Enterprise Cloud. macOS is capped separately at 5, or 50 on Enterprise Your fleet size, and your autoscaler's reaction time. Unlimited in theory, queued in practice Not published by most vendors; Blacksmith states it imposes none. Latchkey sets 20, 40 or 80 busy runners per workspace by plan Where jobs run GitHub's own hosted fleet Your infrastructure, your VPC, your network position. This is the reason most regulated teams are here The vendor's cloud, or your own account on the vendors that offer a bring-your-own-cloud mode Self-healing or retries None. A failed job waits for a person, or for retry logic you wrote yourself None, and the runner host is now also yours to fix when it wedges, fills up or goes offline mid-job Latchkey diagnoses and retries transient failures inside the run; most managed vendors do not offer this Setup change required None; this is the default Runner agents, an autoscaler, images, patching, secrets rotation, disk cleanup, plus a runs-on label A runs-on label change, and for some vendors a GitHub App install GitHub-hosted: the default, and why it stops being free The standard runner is the whole story. On a private repository it is 2 vCPU, 8 GB of RAM and 14 GB of SSD; on a public repository the same ubuntu-latest label gives 4 vCPU and 16 GB, free and unlimited. That asymmetry is why a workflow gets slower the week a repository is made private. The bill arrives from two directions. Minutes are rounded up per job, so a matrix of forty 70-second jobs bills as 80 minutes rather than 46.7. And the included allowance is a dollar amount, deducted at each runner's per-minute rate, so a Team plan's $18 covers 3,000 standard Linux minutes at $0.006 but only about 290 macOS minutes at $0.062. The ceilings are the other half: 14 GB of disk is why no space left on device is so common, and 8 GB of RAM is why exit code 137 turns up on builds that were fine last quarter. Self-hosted: cheap compute, expensive attention GitHub charges nothing for self-hosted Actions usage; its billing page says so in as many words. What you pay instead is your cloud bill plus the part nobody costs in advance: the autoscaler that has to be right, the images that drift, the disk that fills because a persistent BuildKit cache is why you self-hosted, and the runner that goes offline halfway through a release. The economics only work at high utilisation. A fleet sized for your worst hour is mostly idle for the other twenty-three, and idle bills. Ephemeral autoscaled runners fix that and reintroduce the cold start you were avoiding, in exchange for the strongest security posture of the three models, because nothing survives between jobs. None of this argues against self-hosting. It argues for being honest about why. There are four good reasons: hardware nobody rents, a network position you need, a compliance answer that requires jobs inside your own account, and volume large enough that a flat cloud commitment beats any metered rate. "It is cheaper" is not one of them on its own, because it is only cheaper once you refuse to count your own time. Managed runners: the model that did not exist for the original question A managed runner vendor operates the fleet and sells you the minutes. To the workflow it is indistinguishable from GitHub-hosted: same actions, same secrets, same matrix, one different label. To the invoice it is closer to self-hosted, because you pay compute rates rather than platform rates. The category is crowded enough to have shape. Blacksmith and Depot sell runners on their own hardware with arm64, Windows and macOS. Namespace sells shapes and cache volumes on a prepaid plan. RunsOn and the bring-your-own-cloud modes run the fleet inside your AWS account, a hybrid of this model and the last. Latchkey sells Linux x64 only and adds what none of the others do: diagnosing a transient failure and retrying it inside the run. The honest cost of this model is vendor risk, and it is not theoretical: BuildJet shut down in March 2026 and Cirrus CI followed in June. The mitigation is the thing that makes adoption cheap. Because it is a label, leaving is a label. Cost: the same month under all three models Ten thousand Linux minutes at 2 vCPU plus two thousand macOS minutes a month, on a private repository. The self-hosted row is the only one where the published price is not the price. Linux compute macOS compute What else you pay Monthly total $60 at $0.006/min $124 at $0.062/min Nothing $184 Your instance rate for the hours the fleet is up, not the minutes jobs run Apple hardware or a licensed Mac cloud; the most expensive thing to self-host Autoscaler, images, patching, disk cleanup, and the pager Not publishable: it is your cloud bill plus your time Managed (Latchkey) $25 at $0.0025/min Not offered: $124 on GitHub-hosted $5 to $49 a month for the plan, plus seats past the plan's own at $5 $149 plus the plan The row that will not resolve to a number is the point of the table, not a gap in it. Self-hosted cost is dominated by utilisation and by engineering hours, and both of those are yours. Measure it rather than guess: the hours your fleet was up last month times your instance rate, plus the hours your team spent on it. Teams that do this honestly find the compute was the small half. Two things make self-hosting look better than that sounds: GitHub charges nothing for the Actions usage itself, and a warm disk with a persistent build cache is worth real minutes on a Docker-heavy pipeline. The managed row is gross too: its plan fee is separate from the compute, and its 2,000 to 6,000 included minutes are not netted off. Speed Not benchmarked yet; the runner benchmark report will replace this section. There is no honest ranking without running the same workload on all three, and the number everyone quotes is a vendor multiple measured on a workload the vendor chose. What the published specifications do say: a standard private-repo GitHub-hosted runner is the smallest machine of the three at 2 vCPU and 8 GB, a self-hosted runner is as fast as whatever you buy and starts warm if it is long-lived, and managed vendors sell larger sizes at lower rates than GitHub's larger runners. Reliability Each model fails differently, and that is more useful than any uptime number. GitHub-hosted fails as an opaque platform incident you wait out. Self-hosted fails as your infrastructure: a full disk, a wedged agent, a runner that lost communication mid-job and took the run with it. Managed runners fail as a vendor incident, plus the risk the vendor leaves the market. All three behave the same on a bad job: a registry timeout or an out-of-memory kill bills, and the re-run bills again. Self-hosting makes this worse rather than better, because host state joins your failure surface. To size that line item before you pick a model, count the runs in your Actions history that passed on a second attempt with no code change in between. When to choose each GitHub-hosted when your repositories are public, when your minutes fit the included allowance, when your bill is mostly macOS (it is the cheapest macOS of the three), or when adding a vendor would mean redoing a compliance answer. Self-hosted when you need hardware nobody rents, a network position inside your own VPC, jobs inside your own account for compliance, or a persistent build cache on a long-lived host. Budget the fleet as infrastructure, because that is what it is. Managed when the answer to "why are we self-hosting" is only ever cost, when your Linux bill has outgrown the included allowance, or when you want larger machines without operating them. Check the vendor's OS coverage first: Latchkey is Linux x64 only, so a macOS or Windows job stays where it is. Switching: the exact diff Moving between GitHub-hosted and managed is one line per job. Moving to self-hosted is one line per job plus a fleet, which is the asymmetry the table cannot show. jobs: test: - runs-on: ubuntu-latest + runs-on: latchkey-medium # managed: label only gpu-eval: + runs-on: [self-hosted, linux, gpu] # plus an agent, an image and an autoscaler ios: runs-on: macos-latest # left alone: cheapest macOS of the three The verdict Stay on GitHub-hosted if your repositories are public or your minutes fit the allowance, because nothing paid competes with free and the default costs you no decision. Self-host when you have a reason that is not cost, which means hardware, network position, compliance or a persistent cache, and budget it as infrastructure with a person attached rather than as a saving. For everyone else, and that is most teams, managed runners are the model the original question did not have: self-hosted economics, no fleet, and a runs-on line you can revert in a minute if it disappoints. The caveats are real and worth saying out loud. Managed vendors leave the market, most of them cover only some operating systems, and none of the three models, on its own, does anything about the job that failed at 2am for a reason that had nothing to do with your code. FAQ When should you use self-hosted runners vs GitHub-hosted runners? Self-host when you need something GitHub does not rent: GPUs or other specific hardware, a network position inside your own VPC, jobs in your own account for compliance, or a persistent build cache on a long-lived host. Stay GitHub-hosted when your repositories are public, your minutes fit the allowance, or your bill is mostly macOS. Choosing self-hosted purely to save money usually means the ops time has not been counted. Per minute charges for self hosted runners? GitHub's billing page states that Actions usage is free for self-hosted runners, as read on 20 September 2026. What you pay is your cloud provider's instance rate for the whole time the fleet is up, not just the minutes jobs run, which is why utilisation rather than rate decides whether self-hosting is cheaper. Which GitHub Actions services let you run jobs on faster hardware without self-hosting? Managed runner vendors: Blacksmith, Depot, Namespace, WarpBuild, Ubicloud, RunsOn and Latchkey, plus GitHub's own larger runners, which go to 96 vCPU on x64. All of them are adopted with a runs-on label change, and the vendors are typically cheaper per minute than GitHub's larger runners at the same size. What hardware do GitHub-hosted runners actually give you? On a private repository the standard Linux runner is 2 vCPU, 8 GB of RAM and 14 GB of SSD. On a public repository the same label gives 4 vCPU and 16 GB, free and unlimited. Windows matches Linux, and macOS on Apple silicon is 3 vCPU with 7 GB. The 14 GB of disk is the same on all of them, which is why disk-full failures appear on jobs with plenty of memory. References GitHub Actions billing, including self-hosted runners and cache allowance GitHub Actions runner pricing: per-minute rates GitHub-hosted runner specifications GitHub Actions usage limits and concurrency Latchkey runner sizes and rates

articles.title: Jira Sandbox to Production: What the Deploy Beta Checks
articles.description: On 6 July 2026 Atlassian's product manager for sandboxes posted on the Community that Jira and Jira Service Management admins could deploy configuration changes from a sandbox to production, as an open beta. By 14 November that post had 8,965 views. Atlassian's docs say it deploys workflows, fields, screens, schemes, boards, filters and automation rules to production without an app, for org admins on Premium or Enterprise. It's one-way, though: the review screen says deployed changes "can't be reversed". We tried it on 14 November on our own organization, and we stopped at the review screen, before the deploy button. We picked 4 changes, the tool counted 110 items to deploy, and 12 of them showed errors. The one warning we read named a field called Story Points that exists on both of our sites, and the fix the screen suggests is a full copy of production into the sandbox, which overwrites everything in it. A sandbox, if you haven't opened one yet, is a separate Jira site linked to your production site, for testing changes before your users see them. Ours is Premium, with production on wolfaenpak.atlassian.net and the sandbox on leanzero-demo.atlassian.net. Below are the steps with our real screens and timings, then Atlassian's own list of what moves and what doesn't. If you'd rather copy whole projects between two Cloud sites, that's a different job, covered in merge two Jira Cloud instances. What we found when we tried it on 14 November 2026 The first scan of our sandbox, which had never been copied from production, took about 13 minutes and listed 764 differences. Selecting 4 items selected 16, and validation then counted 110, most of them fields that our project's field scheme depends on. 12 of the 110 showed errors, our project among them, so the part we cared about couldn't go. We didn't start the deployment. Production had 0 new fields, statuses, workflows, filters or projects afterwards, and the moved-or-not table below is Atlassian's documentation. Before you start: role, plan and a fresh copy Note Prerequisites — you need all of this before step 1. Role: organization admin. Site admins can't deploy, and a public suggestion to change that, CLOUD-13068, is open. Plan: Jira or Jira Service Management on Premium or Enterprise. Premium includes 1 sandbox per app and Enterprise up to 5 (Understand billing for sandboxes). Cloud only, and not Atlassian Government Cloud, where deployment isn't available (Deploy configuration changes from a sandbox). Company-managed projects only. Team-managed projects aren't supported (Data deployed from sandboxes). A recent full copy of production in the sandbox. Without one the scan still runs, as ours did, but Atlassian says deployments only work accurately after it. Step 1 checks this. When you're done you'll have a validated deployment, and you'll know which items will reach production and which ones need fixing first. The procedure at a glance [[steps]] Check the sandbox's last copy — compare Last data copy with the cut-off dates and refresh if it's older. Make your changes in the sandbox — in a company-managed project, with names you can search for. Create a deployment — pick your production site and let the scan run. Find your changes — search the scan and rescan if something is missing. Select and check dependencies — tick your items and look at what the tool adds. Review and read every error — open the side panel of each item with an error. Start the deployment and read the report — then confirm one item in production. You should see the same seven stages in the admin screens, in this order. Step 1: Check the Jira sandbox's last refresh (its copy of production data) Atlassian says deployments only work accurately after a recent full copy. Without one, items made separately on each site look new: in our never-copied sandbox 752 of the 764 differences were Added, and Story Points was flagged as a same-name duplicate. It still scanned, so the copy isn't required to start, only to get a clean result. In admin.atlassian.com, select Apps, then Sandboxes. The page lists your sandboxes with a Last data copy column. Read Last data copy on your Jira sandbox's row. Ours said Never copied. Compare it with the cut-off dates on the banner of a new deployment (step 3 shows where). Ours asked for a copy "on or after February 7, 2026 for deploying Jira configurations (excluding automations), or May 17, 2026 for deploying Jira Service Management configurations and any automation rules." Atlassian's recommended workflow page says May 7 for the second date. If your copy is dated between 7 and 17 May 2026, the docs accept it but the screen doesn't, so make a new one. Optional: to refresh, select More actions (…) on the row, then Copy production data. The copy options open. Optional: choose All projects, then Copy data with attachments or Copy data without attachments. A summary of the data to copy appears. Optional: review the summary and select Copy data. The copy starts. You should see a Last data copy date after the cut-off. Ours didn't have one. A copy replaces everything in the sandbox, and a full copy into one Jira-family sandbox also overwrites your Jira Service Management and Product Discovery sandboxes, if you have them (How do sandboxes work for the Jira family of apps?). So refresh first, then build. We skipped the copy on purpose. Our sandbox holds the demo data for our own apps, and a copy would have wiped it. That choice probably explains what happened in step 6, so with a fresh sandbox you should get further than we did. Step 2: Make your changes in the sandbox Open your sandbox site and make the configuration changes you want to ship, in a company-managed project. Give them names you can search for later. We started every name with SBX, a prefix we made up, so we could find each item, and later delete it, by name. Our test was a company-managed project called SBX Deploy Test. It got its own workflow with a new status, SBX Review, and a validator that makes a field required before review. We added a dropdown field, a screen, a filter shared with the project, a project role and an automation rule that comments on new work items. Step 3: Create a Jira sandbox deployment and choose production On the Sandboxes page, select More actions (…) on your Jira sandbox's row. The menu shows Create a deployment with a Beta label. Select Create a deployment. A deployment page opens, named after the date and time. Ours was "November 14, 2026_11:21:37_Jira_Deployment". Under Destination, select Select destination and pick your production site. Select Confirm. A progress bar appears under Scanning your data. You can leave the page while it scans. View deployment log in the same menu shows the status "scanning data". Our first scan, run before step 2, took about 13 minutes and listed 764 differences, 752 added and 12 modified. With a sandbox that has never been copied, nearly everything looks new. Step 4: Find your changes in the scan In Search entity name, type a word from your changes. We typed SBX. Read the groups. Each one is an item type with a count (Atlassian calls each configuration item an entity, and a board shows up as Rapid View). A green plus means added and a pencil means modified. If a change is missing, select Scan again, then Begin scan in the dialog. A rescan clears your selection. Our changes came after the first scan, so we rescanned. It took 5.4 minutes, the total rose from 764 to 785, and the search found 19 SBX items, all of them Added. The automation rule was there too. Step 5: Select your changes and check the dependencies Tick the items you want to deploy. We ticked 4: the project, the filter, the project role and the automation rule. Select the Selected tab. Ours showed 16, because the tool ticks what those 4 depend on. Optional: select an item's name to open its side panel. Dependencies lists what it needs and Used by lists what needs it. So the selection grows fast, from 4 to 16 in our case. You should see your own items plus the ones they need. The help page puts it simply: "we automatically select any configuration dependencies". Step 6: Review the deployment and read every error Select Review Deployment. A progress bar shows Validating entities. Ours took about 2.5 minutes. Read the summary at the top. Ours said "12 errors found", with All 110, Ready for deployment 98 and Contains errors 12. Select Contains errors. Each item with a problem carries a red Contain errors badge. Select an item's name. The side panel's Overview tab explains the error. The jump from 16 to 110 happens here. Validation followed the chain one level further. Our project uses the default field scheme, whose panel lists 74 dependencies, and the review counted 72 fields, so most of the jump is likely that scheme. The 12 items with errors were our automation rule, the field Story Points, the default field configuration, the default field layout scheme, the default field scheme, the default priority scheme, our project (106 dependencies), its board, the Story work type, the project's work type scheme, our workflow and our workflow scheme. We opened the panel for Story Points. It showed a red "Error in dependent entities" box and a yellow warning: Another Field with the same name was created on the destination after the sandbox was last refreshed. Deploying this entity may create a duplicate on the destination, which you can manually clean up post the deployment. To check a name clash yourself, look the field up by name on both sites with the REST API (use your own site and credentials): curl -s -u you@example.com:$API_TOKEN "https://your-site.atlassian.net/rest/api/3/field/search?query=Story%20Points" | jq -r '.values[] | "\(.id) \(.name)"' You should see each field's id and name. Run against our production site and then our sandbox on 14 November, it printed: == wolfaenpak customfield_10054 Story Points == leanzero-demo customfield_10077 Story Points customfield_10153 Story Points So Story Points really is separate fields with one name on our sites, and our sandbox even has two of them, because it was never copied from production. We didn't open the other 11 panels, so we can't tell you which item holds the first error. A name clash like this one is probably the cause, and the panel's own advice is a full copy from production. The red box on the review screen offers Remove and revalidate, which it says removes the 12 items and checks the rest again. When we selected it, we landed back on the selection screen with all 110 still selected. Removing them would have dropped the project and the rule we came to test, and still sent the other 71 fields. So we stopped. Then we deleted our test items from the sandbox. Step 7: Start the deployment and download the report We didn't run this step, so here's Atlassian's procedure from Deploy configuration changes from a sandbox. On the review screen, once no errors are left, select Start Deployment. The deployment runs. On the Sandboxes page, select More actions (…) on the sandbox row, then View deployment log. Your deployment is listed with its status. Select More actions (…) on your deployment, then View details. The details page opens. Select Download report. You get Summary.csv and RequiresAttention.csv. Atlassian asks you to "go through" both files "to check if there are any failures that you might want to address". Then open one of the deployed items in production, a workflow or a field, to confirm it's there. The log page says its details stay available for 14 days. What moves from a Jira sandbox to production, and what stays behind Atlassian's Data deployed from sandboxes page lists what deploys and gives a workaround for each gap. I've put the Jira part in one table. We stopped at review, so none of these rows is measured by us, and I'd treat them as Atlassian's promise until you've seen your own report. Change in the sandbox Deploys? What Atlassian says to do New custom field and its context, field scheme, screen, screen scheme, workflow, workflow scheme, status, priority, work type, work type scheme, project role, board, notification or permission scheme Yes A scheme's link to an existing project changes only if you also select the project New company-managed project Yes, its configuration, no work items The beta announcement: "This does not include issue data" New automation rule Yes, but connections don't "Manually reconfigure connections in automations in the destination" New filter Yes, as private "Manually change the permissions of the filter in the destination" Removing a status from a workflow No Remove it in production by hand Removing a field option or a default value Changing a field's type Change it in production by hand Renaming a project or changing its key Work type icons and other media Upload them in production Anything in a team-managed project Not supported Locked or app-managed fields "Make changes to these custom fields fields directly on production" Deletions don't travel either: "Your deployment won't include any entities deleted on the sandbox", says the recommended workflow page. Marketplace app configuration isn't on Atlassian's list. One admin's field report says "Some of the marketplace app-provided configuration arrived. Some did not arrive at all", with nothing in the result to say which. Atlassian's product manager answered that "marketplace apps config are still a gap". The same report found, deploying into a second sandbox, that a workflow arrived inactive, because the deployment doesn't assign it anywhere. And there's no lock while a deployment runs, according to the suggestion CLOUD-13008. If you run Jira Service Management, note the open bug CLOUD-13024: validation fails for changes to a newly created service space, with no known workaround (In Progress, 16 votes on 14 November). Atlassian's request for app configuration support is CLOUD-12989, with 8 votes. Is there a rollback after a Jira sandbox deployment? The review screen says the changes "can't be reversed", and none of the four help pages on deployment mentions a rollback, undo or revert (we searched each one on 14 November). The admin API behind the page does return fields called canPerformRollback and rollbackAllowedTill. On our deployment, read while it was still scanning, they were false and empty, and I wouldn't plan around them until Atlassian documents them. So treat every deployment as one-way. For Premium, Atlassian suggests you "test your deployment by making changes to a small subset of data before the main deployment or purchase an additional sandbox for testing". What a Jira sandbox costs at 50 and 200 users You get sandboxes and the deployment with Premium. Atlassian's Jira pricing page showed these US dollar prices on 14 November 2026: Users Standard Premium Difference 50, monthly, per user $9.70 $19.60 $495 a month 200, monthly, per user $8.95 $17.13 $1,636 a month 50, annual (26-50 tier) $4,850 $9,800 $4,950 a year 200, annual (101-200 tier) $18,000 $34,500 $16,500 a year Premium buys more than sandboxes, so don't read the whole difference as the price of this feature. Our Premium vs Enterprise pricing at 200-500 users goes through the rest. A second sandbox for testing is "$10,000 per sandbox, per app" on annual billing (Atlassian Sandboxes). Configuration tools on the Marketplace are the other route. Appfire's Configuration Manager for Jira lists $1,585 a year at 50 users and $5,120 at 200 in Atlassian's Marketplace pricing data (read 14 November 2026). Salto's own pricing page says "Contact us", and its Marketplace listing shows "Free app". If something doesn't work "Another entity with the same name exists on destination" means an item exists on both sites as two separate items with one name. The panel's advice is a full copy from production into the sandbox. If you deploy anyway, it warns that a duplicate "may" be created in production for you to clean up by hand. Errors on items you didn't pick can come from the dependency chain. In our run the one panel we opened, Story Points, showed "Error in dependent entities" and a same-name warning. Open each panel under Contains errors to find the one with a cause of its own. Your change isn't in the list if you made it after the scan started. Select Scan again, then Begin scan. A new filter is private in production. That's documented behaviour, so share it again by hand. An automation rule uses a connection (Slack, Teams, a web request). Connections don't deploy, so reconfigure them in production. Atlassian doesn't document whether deployed rules arrive enabled. When to use the deploy beta now, and when to wait If your sandbox has a full copy from after the cut-off and your changes live in company-managed projects with no app configuration, I'd use it now. It saves you replaying workflow and field changes by hand, and the review step shows you every dependency before anything moves. Plan the time, though. Our two scans and the validation took about 21 minutes of waiting. If your sandbox is old, or you've been building in it for weeks while production moved on, expect the same name clashes we hit. Refresh first, then build, then deploy. And I'd start with one workflow the first time you try it, because a project pulls in its whole field scheme and we saw how fast that grows. If your workflows lean on Marketplace apps, a manual checklist or a configuration tool is still the safer route. On Standard there's no sandbox at all, so a checklist or a tool is the only route. It's a beta, and the cloud roadmap shows no general availability date. What you have now [[takeaways]] A way to check your sandbox's copy date against the cut-off before you build anything. The scan, select, review and deploy steps, with our real timing for each wait. A REST check that shows whether a field exists twice under one name. Atlassian's list of what deploys and what you'll still fix by hand. It doesn't cover Marketplace app configuration or an undo. You can check your sandbox's copy date, find your changes in a scan, follow the dependencies the tool adds and read validation errors in their side panels. You also have Atlassian's list of what moves and what you'll still fix by hand. If you've run a deployment on a freshly copied sandbox, I'd love to hear what your Summary.csv looked like, because that's the part we couldn't see this time :) Originally published on leanzero.net. More Atlassian, Forge and local-AI write-ups at leanzero.net/blog, and if you're planning a migration or a Forge app, that's what we do: leanzero.net/services.

articles.title: I fixed every dead CTA on my blog. Revenue stayed at zero.
articles.description: I fixed eight call-to-action links on a Saturday night, verified every one against the live page, and my revenue stayed exactly where it was: zero. That is not a failure story. It is what happens when you fix the ceiling of a funnel that has no floor. Here are the numbers, because the numbers are the whole point. The measurement before the fix My dev.to account had 25 published articles and 468 total views, read from the dev.to API on 2026-11-15. Of those 25 articles, 13 linked to a paid product. The other 12 ended with something vague like "follow me for more" and no path whatsoever. That means 217 of 468 views — 46% of everything this account has ever produced — arrived, read, and had nowhere to go. Not a bad offer. No offer. The cheap fix: append a contextual CTA to each article that lacked one. Not a banner, not a popup. A sentence at the end that answers the next question the reader would have, plus a link. The verification that matters more than the edit Eight articles changed. Six of them were re-uploaded through the API, two needed a body patch. Then I did the thing that separates "I edited a file" from "it works": curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{redirect_url}' \ "https://skills.seu.pet/buy/o-agente-que-nao-mente?ref=devto" First attempt returned 303 with the redirect pointing back at /p/o-agente-que-nao-mente. My first read was "the buy route is broken, it's bouncing every buyer back to the product page." It was not broken. The route has an anti-bot guard: if the User-Agent cannot plausibly be a browser, the request is redirected to the product page and no checkout session is created. That guard exists because on 24 October there were 100 Stripe sessions in four days with zero payments, clustered between 3 and 5 AM — link scanners, not shoppers. A curl with its default UA will always look like a scanner. With a real browser UA: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 ... Chrome/131.0 -> 303 https://checkout.stripe.com/g/pay/cs_live_... cs_live_ — a real session on the live account. Two SKUs tested, both live. The route was fine the whole time; my probe was wrong. Rule from this: when you test a purchase path with curl, you are also testing the bot filter. Fake the browser or you will spend an hour debugging a guard that is doing its job. The number that did not move After the fix: 21 of 25 articles carry a paid link, and 467 of 468 views now land on an article with a purchase path. Coverage went from 54% to 99.8%. Paid orders: still zero. Revenue: still R$ 0,00. The reason is one line from my own store's database, measured the same morning: Metric Value Source Human visitors, 30 days 31 orders.db, visitante='humano' Leads, 30 days 2 same Paid orders, 30 days 0 Stripe API, payment_status=paid Stripe sessions, 30 days 558 Stripe /v1/checkout/sessions Google clicks / impressions 5 / 742 Search Console, 2026-11-15 02:48 Thirty-one humans in thirty days. At a realistic 2–3% session-to-purchase rate, 31 visitors produce between 0.6 and 0.9 orders per month. The expected value rounds to zero, and the measured value is zero. Nothing is broken; the arithmetic simply never had a chance. The 558 Stripe sessions look like demand and are not. All 558 are open or expired, none has payment_status=paid, none has a customer e-mail, none has a client_reference_id, and the timestamps are spread uniformly across 24 hours. Human purchases cluster. Machine traffic does not. What the dashboard told me, and what it cost me to believe it My own OpenPanel funnel for the same 30 days reads: 27 page_view -> 26 checkout_start (96.3%) -> 0 purchase (0.0%) A 96% view-to-checkout rate is a fantasy, and I wrote the script that emits it. checkout_start fires when the checkout endpoint is hit, and the checkout endpoint gets hit by the sitemap crawler, by my own probes, and by link scanners. A funnel step that any machine can trigger is not a funnel step, it is a counter. The honest version of that funnel is the one Stripe returns, and Stripe says: 558 attempts, 0 payments, and the attempts were not people. The uncomfortable conclusion A conversion-rate problem and a traffic problem produce the same output — zero revenue — and only one of them is fixable by editing a page. I spent the first part of the week assuming it was the page, because editing a page is something I control. It was not the page. The page converts fine for the traffic it gets: 26 of 27 visitors opened a checkout, even if the majority of that traffic was automated noise. What is missing is the denominator. Thirty-one people, in a month, across five domains. So the CTA fix stays — it is correct, it is verified, and it removes a real leak. But it is not the unlock, and I am not going to pretend it was. What I am doing instead One entry point per article, one contextual exit, and a number I can actually defend. If you are in the same hole, the order that worked for me is: Prove the purchase path responds with cs_live_ using a browser UA, before writing anything about conversion. Compare your funnel count to the payment provider's count. If they disagree, the provider is right. Only then look at the top of the funnel — and accept that "no traffic" is a legitimate diagnosis. If you want the gate that fails a build when a claimed result is not backed by evidence, the AI Test Loop skill is free and it is the tool I use for exactly this: AI Test Loop — free download If you would rather read the whole method end to end — proving the work was done, in fourteen chapters — the ebook is here: O agente que não mente — R$ 37 And if your funnel reports a rate above 90% on any step between "page loaded" and "money arrived", go check what fires that event. It is probably not a person.

articles.title: GitHub Actions YAML anchors, aliases, and the merge key that is not one
articles.description: GitHub Actions YAML anchors are documented as usable on GitHub.com, and have been since September 2025, which reverses years of advice saying they are not. What has not changed is the merge key: the documentation shows only anchors and aliases, and the workflow schema has no property to receive a key written as two angle brackets. Anchors and aliases have a documented section for GitHub.com. The merge key appears in neither the documentation nor the schema, and is refused where it lands on a fixed mapping. What this error means One of three things. An anchor and alias pair works fine and you were told it could not, which is the happy case and usually means you are reading an older answer. Or the workflow is rejected with a sentence about anchors not being supported, which points at the product or the parser doing the reading rather than at your file. Or the anchors resolve, the merge key does not, and you get an annotation naming a key you did not think you had written. ```Message text from YamlObjectReader in actions/runner, the legacy path Anchors are not currently supported. Remove the anchor 'common' ## Common causes ### The advice you found predates the documented support For years the correct answer was that workflows did not take anchors, and a great deal of writing says so. The reference page now carries a section describing them, gated to GitHub.com and Enterprise Cloud, so the old answer is no longer the whole answer. ### A merge key was used to extend a map rather than replace it The merge key is a separate convention from anchors and aliases, it is absent from the documentation, and the schema has no property for it. Where it lands on a fixed mapping it is rejected by name, which reads as a strange error about a key you did not write. ### The file runs somewhere the section does not apply The documentation section is conditioned on GitHub Free, Pro, Team and Enterprise Cloud. A workflow shared with an Enterprise Server installation is outside what the documentation claims, so reuse that works in one place should not be assumed to work in the other. ### An alias refers to an anchor that is not in the same file Aliases are resolved within one document. In our experience this arrives when a workflow is split, because the anchor stays in the file that was not moved and the alias goes with the jobs that were. ## How to fix it ### Use an alias to supply a whole value Anchor a complete map or a complete job and alias it where you want the same thing again, which is exactly what the documented examples do. Replacing a value is supported; extending one is what the merge key was for and there is no substitute for it here. ```.github/workflows/ci.yml (from the documentation's example) jobs: job1: env: &env_vars NODE_ENV: production steps: - run: npm run build job2: env: *env_vars - run: npm test Move shared steps into a composite action When the repetition is a sequence of steps, put them in a composite action and call it. The interface is declared, the reuse crosses files and repositories, and the action appears as its own unit in the run, none of which an alias gives you. ```.github/workflows/ci.yml (illustrative) uses: ./.github/actions/setup with: node-version: '22' ``` Move a shared job into a reusable workflow Add on: workflow_call to the file holding the job, with any inputs it needs declared and typed. Call it from the other workflows with uses at job level. Pass values through with rather than through an alias, so the contract is visible on both sides. Keep anchors for small repetitions inside one file, where they cost nothing to read. Check where the file will run before relying on anchors If the same workflow is used on Enterprise Server as well as GitHub.com, treat anchors as unavailable, because the documentation section that describes them is not published for that product. Reusable workflows and composite actions carry no such condition. How to prevent it Keep anchors to small repetitions inside one file, and reuse across files with uses. Never use a merge key in a workflow, in any position. Note in a comment when a file depends on anchors, so a move to another product is a decision. Prefer a declared interface over textual reuse whenever anyone else will edit the file. What the documentation now says, and for which products The reference page on reusing workflow configurations carries a section headed YAML anchors and aliases. It explains that an anchor marked with an ampersand identifies content you want to reuse and an alias marked with an asterisk repeats it elsewhere, links the YAML specification, and gives two worked examples: one sharing an env map between two jobs, and one reusing an entire job configuration. That section is recent, and it is datable. The commit history of that file in github/docs reaches back to 17 September 2025, and the commit that starts it adds the heading, the opening sentence, both worked examples and the version condition in one change. So the documentation has said this since September 2025, and an answer written before then is not wrong about its own moment. What that date fixes is the documentation rather than the runtime: it says when GitHub started publishing the claim, not when any parser changed, and the claim on this page is the documentary one. The gating on that section is worth reading as carefully as the text. The page as a whole is published for GitHub Free, Pro and Team, for Enterprise Cloud and for Enterprise Server, but the anchors section is wrapped in a condition that selects only the first two. The intro sentence of the page carries the same condition, mentioning anchors and aliases only on those products. So the documentation does not claim the feature for Enterprise Server, and an answer that says anchors work should say where. On the parser side, the workflow parser published in actions/runner has a parse option named AllowAnchors. When it is off, the reader raises the message quoted above for an anchor on a scalar, on a mapping start or on a sequence start. When it is on, the reader records anchors by position and replays them when it meets an alias, and raises a different message for an alias whose anchor it has never seen. GitHub's pre-run validation service is not open, so this page does not claim which setting that service uses; it reports what the published parser offers and what the documentation states. Construct In the documentation In the published schema &name anchor a section, gated to GitHub.com and Enterprise Cloud handled by the reader, behind a parse option *name alias the same section, with two examples replayed from the recorded anchor << merge key not mentioned anywhere no property, and no loose key on a job An alias with no anchor not mentioned the reader raises an unknown anchor error The merge key is not a parser feature. YAML anchors and aliases are defined by the parsing layer, while the merge key is a convention applied above it, so a reader can support the first two and still deliver the third as an ordinary key named with two angle brackets. Where a merge key is refused and where it is quietly accepted Because the merge key arrives as an ordinary key, what happens to it depends on the mapping it lands in. The workflow root is a mapping with a fixed set of properties and no loose keys, and a job is a choice between two mappings that also have fixed properties and no loose keys. A key of two angle brackets matches no property in either place, so the reader raises its Unexpected value for it, naming the key. Some mappings are not fixed. A workflow level env map takes any non-empty string as a key, which means a merge key written there is accepted as the name of an environment variable. Nothing fails, and a variable with a peculiar name is created. That is the version of this that is hardest to notice, because the only symptom is that the values you expected to merge are absent. The practical rule is to use anchors and aliases to replace a whole value and never to extend one. Aliasing a complete env map onto a second job is what the documented examples do. Splicing extra keys into an existing map is the thing the merge key was for, and there is nothing in the workflow language that does it. test: &base_job runs-on: ubuntu-latest - uses: actions/checkout@v7 alt-test: *base_job ## What anchors do not give you An alias is textual reuse inside one file, resolved before anything about workflows is considered. It cannot cross file boundaries, so it is no help at all for sharing configuration between repositories or even between two workflow files in the same repository. It does not deduplicate a matrix. And because the expansion happens before the schema is applied, an alias that produces an invalid shape produces an ordinary schema error at the aliased position, which can be a long way from the anchor that caused it. For reuse across files, the mechanisms are reusable workflows called with `uses` at job level, and composite actions called with `uses` at step level. Both are checked, both have declared interfaces, and both appear in the run as distinct units, which anchors do not. The honest summary is that anchors have become available for the small case they are good at, removing a little repetition within one file, and they have not replaced anything. If you were planning to restructure a repository around them, plan around reusable workflows instead. ## Why there is no recorded run on this page The subject of this page is a difference between products and between eras, and a runner cannot record either. A green run on GitHub.com proves nothing about the same file on Enterprise Server, which is precisely the boundary the documentation draws with its version condition, and no Latchkey runner has an Enterprise Server to compare against. The claims that matter are therefore documentary and source level: a documentation section with a stated version gate, a parse option with a default, and two reader paths with distinct messages. Recording a workflow that happens to work today would invite exactly the mistake this page exists to correct, which is treating one observation of one product as a rule. ## FAQ ### Do YAML anchors work in GitHub Actions workflows? The reference page on reusing workflow configurations documents them, with examples for sharing an env map and for reusing a whole job. That section arrived in September 2025. It is published for GitHub Free, Pro and Team and for Enterprise Cloud, and it is not published for Enterprise Server, so the answer depends on where the workflow runs. ### Can I use the YAML merge key in a workflow? No. The merge key is a separate convention from anchors and aliases, the documentation never mentions it, and the schema has no property for it. Written on the workflow root or on a job it is rejected as an unexpected key, and written in a map that takes loose keys it becomes an ordinary key with a strange name. ### What does "Anchors are not currently supported" mean? It is the message the published workflow parser raises when it meets an anchor and its AllowAnchors option is off. The message names the anchor and asks for it to be removed. GitHub's pre-run validation service is not open source, so what this tells you is what the published parser does, not which setting any particular product uses. ### Should I use anchors instead of reusable workflows? No. An alias is textual reuse inside a single file, resolved before the schema is applied, so it cannot cross files, cannot declare inputs and cannot be checked. Reusable workflows and composite actions do all three, and anchors are best kept for small repetitions within one file. ## References - [GitHub Actions: reusing workflow configurations, YAML anchors and aliases](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/reusing-workflow-configurations) - [actions/runner: YamlObjectReader.cs, the anchor paths](https://github.com/actions/runner/blob/main/src/Sdk/WorkflowParser/Conversion/YamlObjectReader.cs) - [actions/runner: ParseOptions.cs, the AllowAnchors option](https://github.com/actions/runner/blob/main/src/Sdk/WorkflowParser/ParseOptions.cs) - [YAML 1.2.2 specification: node anchors and aliases](https://yaml.org/spec/1.2.2/#3222-anchors-and-aliases) - [github/docs: the commit that added the anchors section, 17 September 2025](https://github.com/github/docs/commit/0c84db7087b2f68cabbe60c87cc0316735f9f6f8)
