articles.title: How a Transliteration Engine Thinks: From "namaste" to Devanagari
articles.description: Most typing tools for Hindi ask you to learn a new keyboard. A transliteration tool takes the opposite bet: you keep typing on the English keyboard you already know, and the software converts your Roman letters into Devanagari script as you go. That sounds simple until you look at the mapping problem: Ambiguity everywhere. A single Roman letter can map to several Devanagari characters depending on context. "a" at the start of a word is not the same as "a" in the middle. Digraphs are units. "kh", "gh", "chh", "aa", "ee" have to be consumed as single sounds, which means the parser should match greedily, longest first. Predictability beats cleverness. Users build a mental model of the tool. If "namaste" converts one way today, it must convert the same way tomorrow, or trust evaporates. The design rule that falls out of all this: the user should never have to think about the machine. They type the way they chat — Hinglish, mixed with English, full of shortcuts — and the script quietly takes care of itself. I work on these problems around a small free tool that does this live in the browser. Type in Hinglish, get Devanagari out, copy it anywhere. No sign-up, no new keyboard, no translation changing your words — just your own sentences in the script they belong to. If you build for multilingual users, I would argue transliteration is the most underrated UX pattern on the web: it meets people at the keyboard they already have.

articles.title: Day Trading vs Settlement: Same-Day US Stock Trades Do Not Mean T+0 Settlement
articles.description: Can you buy and sell a US stock on the same day, and does that mean it settles immediately? Same-day trading can be possible under applicable account rules, but most ordinary US stock transactions use T+1 settlement. Keeping trade date, expected settlement date and confirmed settlement status separate prevents a trading interface from presenting an executed sale as already settled cash. A same-day purchase and sale describe when two trades happen. Settlement describes when the resulting obligations are completed. Calling both processes “T+0” hides a distinction that matters to investors and to the software displaying their accounts. For ordinary US stock transactions covered by the standard cycle, the settlement convention is T+1, not T+0. That does not mean every investor must hold a stock overnight. It means same-day trading permission and settlement timing are different questions. Neither a quote feed nor a successful order submission answers both. What does the T actually measure? In settlement notation, T is the trade date. T+1 means one business day after that date; T+0 would mean settlement on the trade date. Execution time is more precise: it records when an order, or part of an order, was filled. A trade date is a business label, not simply the date shown on the viewer's laptop. The SEC's T+1 transition FAQ identifies May 28, 2024 as the compliance date for the shortened standard cycle. Its guidance also describes exceptions and limited circumstances involving expressly agreed settlement terms. The useful statement is therefore “most ordinary US stock transactions settle on T+1,” not “every security settles tomorrow.” Imagine a hypothetical purchase and sale on the same Monday, with Tuesday an ordinary applicable business day. The trades occur on Monday, while their expected standard settlement date can be Tuesday. Closing the position does not turn Monday into the settlement date. This illustration assumes an ordinary transaction and no intervening holiday; it is not a calendar or account-eligibility calculation. Illustration of ordinary T+1 transactions. Instrument-specific terms and applicable business calendars still matter. Does “same-day trading” mean unlimited trading? No. It describes timing, not permission. Whether an account can enter a transaction depends on its funding, type, restrictions and the broker's current controls. FINRA's current cash-account guidance says securities must be fully paid for before they are sold. For intraday purchases and sales, it emphasizes using settled funds at purchase. It also distinguishes a good-faith violation involving unsettled sale proceeds from free-riding. A screen that shows sale proceeds is not, by itself, proof that those proceeds are settled and available for every subsequent use. Margin accounts follow a different framework. FINRA adopted new intraday margin requirements effective June 4, 2026, with a permitted broker transition period through October 20, 2027. During that transition, generic summaries of historical pattern-day-trader rules are not a reliable substitute for checking the rules a particular broker applies. This article does not calculate buying power or determine whether an account may trade. Frequent trading carries financial risk, and margin can increase losses beyond the original deposit. The distinction explained here is educational, not a recommendation to trade more often or a way to avoid account restrictions. Market data is not your settlement record A market-data message tells you about the market. A broker execution report tells you about your fills. A settlement record tells you the broker-reported state of the resulting obligations. These sources answer different questions even when their timestamps look similar. TickDB's documented US-stock market data is useful for displaying prices and observing market activity. Its ticker documentation includes a market-data timestamp and conditionally available quote fields. Those fields should not be interpreted as proof that your account bought a security, that an order was filled, or that funds have settled. For a portfolio interface, keep the price panel separate from the order and cash ledger. A fresh TickDB quote can update valuation without changing an execution or settlement flag. Likewise, a broker's execution notification should not automatically change a pending-settlement balance into a settled balance. A quote timestamp is not a settlement confirmation. This is an information-model illustration, not a screenshot of a broker system. A small state model that avoids the shortcut The following Python example keeps three facts separate: trade date, an externally supplied expected settlement date, and a confirmation flag. All records are fabricated. The dates are inputs, not a calculation of US holidays or settlement eligibility. from dataclasses import dataclass from datetime import date @dataclass(frozen=True) class TradeRecord: trade_id: str trade_date: date expected_settlement_date: date | None settlement_confirmed: bool = False def display_status(self): if self.settlement_confirmed: return "Broker reported settled" if self.expected_settlement_date is None: return "Settlement date unknown" return f"Expected {self.expected_settlement_date}; not confirmed" # Fabricated records; dates are supplied, never calculated here. buy = TradeRecord("BUY-1", date(2026, 11, 16), date(2026, 11, 17)) sell = TradeRecord("SELL-1", date(2026, 11, 16), date(2026, 11, 17)) assert buy.trade_date == sell.trade_date assert not buy.settlement_confirmed and not sell.settlement_confirmed assert "not confirmed" in sell.display_status() unknown = TradeRecord("UNKNOWN-1", date(2026, 11, 16), None) assert unknown.display_status() == "Settlement date unknown" confirmed = TradeRecord("DONE-1", date(2026, 11, 16), date(2026, 11, 17), True) assert confirmed.display_status() == "Broker reported settled" print(buy.display_status()) print(sell.display_status()) The local example prints the same expected date for both trades, with “not confirmed” attached to each. It also checks an unknown-date case and an explicitly confirmed case. A same-day round trip does not set either confirmation flag. This is deliberately not a brokerage integration. In production, only a validated, appropriately matched broker event should change the confirmation state. Store the source, event identifier and update time so that the interface can explain why it changed. Preserve corrections rather than treating the first notification as permanent truth. Do not replace a missing expected date with “today plus one day.” Weekends are not the only calendar issue, and instrument terms can matter. Do not use the current wall clock passing an expected date as proof of completion either: expected and confirmed remain separate states. If a source is delayed, show that uncertainty instead of manufacturing a settled status. What should the interface actually say? Prefer narrow labels such as “order filled,” “expected settlement date,” “settlement pending,” and “broker reported settled.” Avoid one green “complete” badge that conflates execution, position closure, cash availability and settlement. When explaining a rejection or cash restriction, use the broker's current response and account records, not an inference from the market-data timestamp. When explaining T+1, name the applicable scope and distinguish business days from calendar days. If the needed confirmation is unavailable, “unknown” is more accurate than a confident date-derived answer. The practical answer to the original question is simple: same-day US stock trading does not establish same-day settlement. Treat trading permission, execution and settlement as separate facts, and require the right evidence for each. Official materials checked November 15, 2026: SEC T+1 FAQ, FINRA Frequent Intraday Trading and New Intraday Margin Requirements, and TickDB ticker documentation. The code and diagrams are educational examples, not live account tests or investment advice.

articles.title: Your scraper will not throw an error: designing page extraction that fails loudly, one field at a time
articles.description: A scraper almost never fails the way a program is supposed to fail. It does not raise. It returns a number. Last week a price list came back as 0. The page had been redesigned: the price was still on it, in a that no longer carried the class the extractor looked for. The extractor found nothing, applied .get_text() to nothing, and the pipeline wrote 0 into a table, where 0 is a legal price. Nobody saw the problem until a quote went out at zero. That is the failure mode worth engineering against, and it is not the one most scraping guides prepare you for. An exception is a gift: it stops, it names a line, it leaves a hole you notice. The quiet failures — the empty string, the plausible wrong number, the field that came from the wrong element on the same page — are the ones that travel. This is about extraction that fails loudly, per field, and about the small set of decisions that make a scraper survive the page it reads: where you anchor, what you do when a field is absent, what counts as a change, and how you enumerate a list that is being written while you read it. Three ways an extraction fails, and only one of them is obvious shape what you see what the pipeline does how it's usually found loud an exception, a stack trace stops immediately empty the field is "", [], None writes a row with a hole when a report has a blank column plausible a legal but wrong value continues confidently downstream, by a person, days later Of the three, the loud one is the cheapest and the plausible one is the only genuinely dangerous one. A design that treats all three the same way — "log it and move on" — optimises for the cheapest failure and hides the expensive one. The concrete shapes of plausible are worth naming, because each needs a different guard: A sibling's value. .parent().find("span") returns the first span, and after a layout change the first span is the unit ("per person") instead of the amount. A default. The code has price or 0, or capacity or 4, because some page somewhere was missing the field. The default outlives the reason it was added. A stale value. The page is a cached copy, or the extraction ran against yesterday's fixture. A wrong item. The selector matched the first result rather than the requested one. A unit change. 12,000 → 12.000 after a locale switch, parsed as 12. None of those are visible in an exit code of 0. Keep the page before you parse it The single decision that makes every later question answerable costs almost nothing: store the raw response, with the URL, the fetch time, the status code, and a content hash, before any parsing happens. def fetch(url, session): r = session.get(url, timeout=20) body = r.text rec = { "url": url, "status": r.status_code, "fetched_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(timespec="seconds"), "sha256": hashlib.sha256(body.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest(), "body": body, } store_raw(rec) # append-only, content-addressed return rec Two things become possible once this exists, and neither is possible without it. First, any parse can be replayed. When a field comes back wrong, you do not re-fetch a page that may have changed again; you re-run the extractor against the exact bytes that produced the bad row. That is the difference between a bug you can debug and a bug you can only reproduce by luck. Second, the hash is a free change signal. Identical bytes mean the page did not change, so the extractor's output should be identical; if the output differs, your parser is non-deterministic (iteration order, locale, clock) and that is a real bug. Different bytes with identical output is the normal case for a page carrying a timestamp or a session token — which is why page-level hashing is a poor alert and per-field hashing is a good one. Storage is cheap at this scale: a 120 KB page per fetch, a few hundred fetches a day, is nothing against the cost of reconstructing a page you no longer have. Anchor on the fact, not on the layout Every field should be extracted by a ladder of anchors, in order, and the ladder should be explicit in the code rather than implied by whichever selector happened to work when you wrote it. tier anchor survives breaks when 1 typed data: JSON-LD, microdata, itemprop, data-* the site owns, an API the page itself calls redesigns, CSS refactors the site stops publishing it 2 identity by meaning: a link whose href matches a pattern, an element whose accessible name or aria-label says what it is, a table with header text class renames, markup reshuffles the wording changes 3 label adjacency: find the text "Opening hours", take the value beside it most redesigns the label is reworded or split 4 normalised text patterns: a regex over whitespace-collapsed text near a keyword a lot, for a while too permissive, matches a neighbour And one anchor that should never appear: the positional path. div > div:nth-child(3) > span:nth-child(2) is not an anchor, it is a snapshot of yesterday's layout. It is also the shape that produces plausible wrong values most reliably, because after a redesign it still matches something. The same rule applies to generated class names. css-1x2y3z is a build artefact; it changes when the site's bundler changes, which is more often than the design does. Prefer the attribute that describes the fact over the attribute that describes the styling. A practical check on any selector you are about to commit: if the page's designer changed the visual layout tomorrow without changing the content, would this still match? If the answer is no for a field that matters, the field is one tier too low. Three tiers per field, and a record of which one fired The ladder is only useful if the extractor reports which rung it landed on. A field that normally comes from tier 1 and suddenly comes from tier 4 is a page that has started to drift, visible before it breaks. def extract_field(doc, spec): """spec: {"tier1": fn, "tier2": fn, "tier3": fn, "tier4": fn} -> Field""" for tier in (1, 2, 3, 4): fn = spec.get(f"tier{tier}") if not fn: continue raw = fn(doc) if raw is None: if isinstance(raw, list) and len(raw) > 1: return Field(raw[0], "ambiguous", tier=tier, candidates=raw) return Field(raw, "found", tier=tier) return Field(None, "missing", tier=None) Three details in that small function matter more than they look. Tier order is a preference, not a fallback chain. Tier 1 should be tried first even when it is slower, because it is the tier whose meaning is stated by the site rather than inferred by you. If tier 1 fires 100% of the time, tiers 2–4 are dead code that will quietly rot; if it fires 60%, you have a working page and a drift problem at the same time, which is the useful thing to know. Ambiguity is its own outcome. Two candidates is not "pick the first one". It is a field whose meaning on that page is unclear, and the honest handling is to record both and mark the field, not to gamble. In a price or a date, the first of two candidates is a coin flip that a person will read as fact. missing is not an error and not a value. It is a state, and it should be spelled out — which is the next section. Absent is a value. Zero is a lie The most expensive line of code in a scraper is the one that makes a hole look like data: price = parse_price(node) or 0 # never or 0 collapses "the page said zero", "the page said nothing", "the parser failed", and "the field was not on this page" into one number. Downstream, a filter sorts by price, a quote totals it, and a person signs it. The fix is a small typed result, carried all the way to storage: @dataclass class Field: value: Any status: str # found | missing | ambiguous | malformed | blocked tier: int | None = None candidates: list | None = None note: str = "" # why it is not found def parse_price(node): if node is None: return Field(None, "missing", note="no price element") text = norm(node.get_text()) # collapse whitespace, unify spaces m = re.fullmatch(r"([\d.,]+)\s*(원|KRW|USD|\$)?", text) if not m: return Field(None, "malformed", note=text[:40]) return Field(to_decimal(m.group(1), m.group(2)), "found") Now 0 means zero, and missing means the page did not say. A row with price.status = "missing" is a row that a person can act on: re-fetch, open the page, ask the client. A row with price = 0 is a row that nobody looks at. Two rules that keep this honest in practice: missing must be visibly missing in whatever the human sees — a dash, not a blank cell and not a zero. Blank cells read as "we didn't get to it"; a typographic dash reads as "the page did not say", which is the truth. The status must survive the write. If the database column is price DECIMAL NOT NULL, the status has nowhere to live and will be flattened to 0 by the first INSERT. Either the column is nullable, or there is a companion price_status column. The schema is where this decision is actually made. Two sources on one page: reconcile, don't pick Many pages state the same fact twice — once for humans in the markup, once for machines in JSON-LD, itemprop, or a hydration payload. That redundancy is free verification: extract both and compare. a = jsonld_field(doc, "price") # typed b = dom_field(doc, "price") # rendered if a and b and a.value != b.value: record("disagreement", field="price", typed=a.value, rendered=b.value) Three outcomes, three different meanings: outcome reading both agree strong; two independent renderings of one fact only the typed source has it fine for data, but the person reading the page does not see it — check which one the business means they disagree a real signal: cached data, a promotion applied in one place, or one of your extractors is wrong The disagreement rate is one of the best single numbers a scraping pipeline can report, because it catches the class of failure that no exception ever will. Normalise before you hash Change detection that compares raw strings alerts on everything and is therefore read by nobody. Hash normalised values, per field: collapse whitespace, including the non-breaking space that appears in prices and never in your regex; unify full-width and half-width characters; resolve relative URLs against the page URL before comparing; normalise numbers to a canonical decimal with the unit kept separately (12000 + KRW, not "12,000원"); convert dates to ISO with the page's stated timezone, or record "timezone unknown" explicitly; sort lists whose order carries no meaning, and do not sort ones where order is the fact (a menu's course order, a schedule's sequence). Then one hash per field, and drift is a field-level event: hours changed, price unchanged. That is a sentence a person can act on, unlike "the page changed". A useful companion metric is tier drift: the share of runs where a field was found below its usual tier. A field normally at tier 1 that spends a week at tier 3 is telling you the site is mid-migration, and the ladder is already carrying the weight. That is the moment to add the tier-2 anchor, not after it goes missing. Enumerating a list that is being written The subtle one: reading a paginated collection while the collection changes underneath you. Offset pagination over a list sorted newest-found-first loses and duplicates items, and it loses them silently. The arithmetic is simple. Page 1 gives items 1–20. Before you request page 2 with offset=20, two new items arrive at the top. Everything shifts down by two, so page 2's window now starts at what used to be item 19: you see 19 and 20 again, and the two oldest items you were about to reach fall off the end of your walk. Reported counts look right; two items were never read, and two were read twice. Two fixes, in increasing order of correctness: Key cursor instead of offset. Ask for "items after this one" using a total order the server guarantees, usually (published_at, id): GET /items?before=<published_at>,<id>&limit=20 The cursor is a position in the ordering, not a count from the top, so insertions at the top cannot shift it. This requires that the sort key is stable and unique — which is why (timestamp, id) is the usual pair: timestamps collide, ids do not. Deduplicate by identity anyway. Even with a cursor, an item can be edited and reordered while you walk, so keep a set of ids seen in the run and drop repeats. The count of dropped repeats is itself a metric: rising duplicates mean the ordering is not as stable as you assumed. And a second watermark for updates. If items can be edited rather than just added, "new since last run" misses them, because they are old. That needs a separate pass keyed on updated_at, with its own cursor, and an explicit rule for what happens when a run overlaps the previous one: the later run wins, and the earlier run's rows for the same ids are superseded, not appended. The general principle: a scrape over a moving list needs a position, not a count. Any API that only offers offsets over a frequently-written collection is telling you it will be approximate — say so in the output rather than pretending otherwise. When the page pushes back A 403 or 429 is not a parser failure, and it is not a reason to try harder. It is the other side's answer, and the only correct responses are to slow down, to stop, and to record it as a state. if r.status_code in (403, 429): return Field(None, "blocked", note=f"HTTP {r.status_code}") Practical rules that kept my own runs out of trouble: A per-host budget, not a global one: N requests per minute per host, plus a cap per run. Concurrency multiplies your request rate in ways that a sleep in one worker does not fix. Honour Retry-After when it is given, and treat its absence as a reason to back off exponentially rather than to retry immediately. Never rotate identity to get past a block. Changing user agent, proxy, or account to keep reading a page that refused you is not engineering, it is defeating a decision the operator made — and it is the thing that turns a missing data point into a banned account or a legal problem. The block is information: the page is not yours to read at this rate. Record the refusal, so a gap in the data has a cause in the log: blocked is a state, and a report that says "hours unknown for 3 of 40 shops — rate limited" is honest, while 3 shops with hours = "" are not. Respect for the crawl budget is also self-interest: a scraper that reads politely can run for years, which is worth far more than the hour it saved by hammering. Fixtures are the regression suite, one incident at a time Every time a field breaks, you already have the page — because you stored it. Copy that response into a fixtures directory, name it for the incident, and add one assertion: fixtures/ shop-1234-2026-11-09-price-removed.html shop-1234-2026-11-09.expected.json def test_price_removed_still_reports_missing(): page = load("shop-1234-2026-11-09-price-removed.html") out = extract(page, SPEC) assert out["price"].status == "missing" assert out["name"].value == "…" Two properties make this suite worth more than its size. It is offline, so it runs in milliseconds and never depends on the live site. And it is documentation: the directory listing is the history of every way this site has surprised you, in the order it happened. The assertion to write in almost every case is not "the value is X" but "the status is what it should be" — that a removed element produces missing rather than 0, that a duplicated element produces ambiguous rather than the first candidate, that a blocked response produces blocked rather than an exception that crashes the batch. The numbers that tell you it is rotting A scraper decays from the day it is written. Four metrics make the decay visible before it costs anything: metric action null rate per field this field is missing more often than the page layout explains add the next anchor tier tier-3/4 fire rate drift in progress; the site is migrating inspect a sample page, promote an anchor disagreement rate (typed vs rendered) one extractor is wrong, or the data is inconsistent inspect; do not average them items per page (expected vs seen) enumeration is drifting, or a block is returning a short page check the cursor and the status code All four are cheap to compute from rows you are already storing, and all four are meaningless at the aggregate level: per field and per site, or they say nothing. "94% success" is a number that hides the only field anyone cares about. What this does not fix A page whose meaning changed while its shape stayed. The digits are in the same and now mean the price per month instead of per item. No tier, no hash, no fixture catches that; only reading the page does. A source that is wrong about itself. Extracting a stale price accurately is still a wrong price. Extraction quality is not truth. Permission. A page you are allowed to read and a page you should read are different questions, and the second one is not technical. A site that deliberately changes shape per request. Obfuscated markup, rotating class names, and decoys exist to make extraction expensive. The honest response is a cheaper source — an API, a feed, a phone call — not a longer selector. A missing decision about what to do with a gap. The pipeline can report missing perfectly and still have nowhere to put it. Someone has to decide whether a row with a missing field is written, held, or dropped. Checklist The raw response is stored before parsing, content-addressed, with URL, status and fetch time. Every field has an explicit anchor ladder: typed data → identity by meaning → label adjacency → normalised text. No field is extracted by positional path or generated class name. The extractor records which tier fired, per field. Ambiguity is a status with the candidates kept, not a coin flip. Absent fields are null with a reason, never 0, "", or a default. The storage schema can hold the status; nothing forces a hole into a zero. Where a page states a fact twice, both copies are extracted and disagreements are recorded. Comparison happens on normalised values, hashed per field. Lists are walked by key cursor, deduplicated by id, with a separate watermark for updates. A 403 or 429 is recorded as blocked; identity is never rotated to defeat it. Each incident leaves a fixture, and the assertions are about statuses as much as values. Null rate, tier-fire rate, disagreement rate, and page size are reported per field and per site. Gaps in the output are visible as gaps to the person reading it. None of this makes extraction correct. It makes extraction legible: for any row you can say which element the value came from, how sure the rung says you should be, what the page did when it had nothing to say, and when it last changed its mind. That is the difference between a scraper that fails and a scraper that lies, and only one of those is recoverable. Disclosure: I build small automation tools and write about the parts that break. articles.title: Node.js Storage API Rate Limit Exceeded While Uploading 3 Processed Thumbnails
articles.description: Short answer: throttle thumbnail uploads per tenant, retry only transient 429 responses with exponential backoff, and make the upload key carry the tenant boundary. Then test the storage-to-observability handoff with the same credentials and base URL. A retry policy cannot repair a key design that lets one tenant read another tenant's object. This field guide covers a property-management system that resizes listing photos and exports a tenant's processed images. Run a small experiment: upload the same 24 thumbnail jobs for three tenants, inject a controlled burst, and record pass or fail for isolation, retry behavior, and operator visibility. For this particular seam, Infrai is worth testing as one measured leg: its plain REST API needs no SDK to install, and one key can cover storage plus the operational handoff. That removes client-library version work, but it does not remove tenant authorization or the need to test quotas. The discovery surface is public and self-describing, so the experiment can inspect the documented method and path before it sends tenant data. That is a useful second advantage here: the worker's integration test can catch a contract mismatch before a burst turns it into a rate-limit investigation. Option Pick this when Boundary to verify Amazon S3 You need the broadest storage ecosystem and can assemble the surrounding controls IAM, bucket policy, object prefixes, and export jobs must agree Cloudflare R2 You want an S3-compatible object store close to Cloudflare workloads Check signing, egress, and tenant-policy behavior Google Cloud Storage Your platform already lives in Google Cloud Validate project and object permissions instead of assuming a prefix is isolation One REST surface You want storage and release observability under one key and base URL Test the shared failure and audit path, then accept one vendor, bill, and outage surface The table is a starting point, not a winner announcement. S3 has the deepest surrounding ecosystem. R2 can fit Cloudflare-heavy systems. Google Cloud Storage fits teams organized around Google identity and projects. A single REST surface reduces glue, but it gives you one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. Say that trade-off out loud before the experiment. Which boundary does the experiment prove? Use keys such as tenants/acme/listings/42/thumb-640.webp. The prefix helps diagnosis and listing, but it is not the whole security model. The service must authorize the tenant before it constructs a key or accepts an export request. Keep objects private or signed-only. A permanent public URL is the wrong output for tenant-scoped exports. Define the pass criteria before sending traffic: A tenant can retrieve only its own signed export URLs. A burst produces bounded retries rather than a tight retry loop. A successful upload is visible in the operational record with its tenant and object key. No retry creates a second logical object or advances the rollout twice. Fail the run if any cross-tenant read succeeds. Fail it too if the client retries a 400-level validation error, ignores Retry-After, or hides the final response body. Those are different failures and need different fixes. Why was the storage API rate limit exceeded while uploading thumbnails? A renderer and an uploader are separate jobs. If rendering succeeded, retry the upload; do not render the same image again because the storage request was rate-limited. I initially treated the pipeline as one retryable unit. That repeated the expensive step and obscured which boundary was failing. The smaller unit is easier to reason about. Small bursts are enough to expose this mistake. This example uses the verified object-write path, a private object policy in the surrounding storage configuration, and an idempotency key derived from the tenant and object key. It never sends the service authorization header to a signed URL. The delay has jitter, honors Retry-After, and stops after a finite number of attempts. type UploadInput = { tenantId: string; bucket: string; objectKey: string; bytes: Uint8Array; contentType: string }; Vary concurrency, not just retry counts. Start at one upload per tenant, then try two, four, and eight concurrent uploads while keeping thumbnail bytes and keys fixed. Record status, attempt number, tenant, object key, and final error class. Do not put image bytes or bearer tokens into logs. Where does one key help the release path? After the worker has a successful { tenantId, bucket, objectKey } result, pass that result to the operational event for the rollout that enabled the new thumbnail code path. Storage identifies the artifact; observability tells the operator which tenant and release produced it. Both calls use Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY and https://api.infrai.cc/v1. The shared key is the integration fact worth testing, not a claim that one service removes operational work. The first check can discover the live capability descriptions. The returned path field is the source of truth, so the test does not hard-code a prose description or invent a route. Infrai is the option I would try for this handoff when the team values one plain HTTP interface across both steps; the reason is fewer client integrations, not a claim that one service removes operational work. type Capability = { path: string; method: string; module: string }; With Neon or PlanetScale plus LaunchDarkly, the same plan means two signups, two credential sets, and glue you own: snapshot or branch coordination, flag-state correlation, event identity, and dashboards that agree about the rollout. That stack can be better when a team already has those systems or needs their specialist features. The single-key path fits only when the seam between artifact storage and release visibility is the problem being simplified. What should each option own? Keep the storage provider responsible for object bytes, private access, and signed delivery. Keep the application responsible for tenant authorization, idempotent job identity, and the export manifest. Keep observability responsible for enough context to investigate a 429 without leaking credentials. Compare the same workload against S3, R2, and Google Cloud Storage using each provider's documented quota and retry guidance. Choose the option that passes every isolation test, keeps retry volume bounded under the expected burst, and leaves an operator with a readable failure trail. If several pass, prefer the one whose identity and export controls match the existing operating model. There are hard limits. Private, signed-only storage does not provide a permanent public image URL. Without object versioning or object lock, an accidental overwrite is not an immutable record. Strict conditional-write coordination needs a queue or database because an If-Match write is not available. Browser direct uploads need a platform with self-service CORS configuration. Lifecycle expiration is measured in days, not hours, and metadata is not a server-side search index. These boundaries make a specialist provider better for public image hosting, WORM retention, complex cross-region replication, or browser-first upload policy. For this workflow, try the one-key path for the storage-to-observability experiment only if tenant authorization remains in the application and the pass criteria stay visible. Start with the storage documentation, then verify provider quotas and retry guidance before increasing concurrency. For this workflow, Infrai is a candidate for teams that want the storage-to-observability experiment behind one REST key and one bill, and can accept one vendor and shared operational dependency. In a property platform, that means the thumbnail worker and the release record do not each need a separate credential inventory or a hand-written reconciliation job just to explain which tenant's artifact entered a rollout. The application still owns authorization, and the experiment still has to prove isolation. This is a narrower benefit than “use one service for everything”: it removes one class of integration glue at the exact storage-observability seam under test. Then stop. articles.title: Your RAG Agent Is Quoting Deleted Documents (Postgres + pgvector Fix)
articles.description: Your AI agent just quoted a contract to a customer. That contract was terminated six weeks ago and deleted from Postgres the same day. Its embedding wasn't. It was still sitting in a separate vector database, and nobody owned the sync job. Two databases, one sync job Most RAG tutorials start the same way: documents live in Postgres, and their embeddings go to a dedicated vector database. Two systems means a sync job. Every insert, update and delete has to reach both, in order, or your agent retrieves things that no longer exist. It also means two security models. Postgres knows this user can only see their own company's contracts. The vector database doesn't, so permissions get copied into metadata filters, and the copies drift. And every question pays two round trips: one to find similar chunks, another to fetch the real rows. For most enterprise workloads there's a simpler answer: keep the embeddings next to the data they describe. One database: data and embeddings One Postgres database holds the documents, the tenants, the permissions and, with the pgvector extension, the embeddings. Same rows, same transactions, same backups. When a document changes, the change and an outbox event commit together. An embedding worker picks up the event, calls the embedding model and writes the vectors back. It's the same queue-and-worker pattern from the previous article on AI middleware. Delete a document and its embeddings go with it; there's nothing left to orphan. At query time the RAG API runs one SQL query that applies similarity, business filters and permissions together. Row-level security covers vectors exactly like it covers everything else. The best chunks then go to the LLM as context. The schema Store chunks, not one embedding per document. A 40-page contract has to be split, or the one paragraph that matters gets averaged away. Each chunk references its document with ON DELETE CASCADE. Delete the contract, and every chunk and every vector goes with it, in the same transaction. That's the bug from the opening, gone at the schema level. Three more details: The vector dimension must match your embedding model (1536 here). An HNSW index with cosine distance. Without it, every query scans every row. Row-level security, so every query on this table, vector search included, only sees the current tenant's rows. -- schema.sql CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector; CREATE TABLE doc_chunks ( id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, doc_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES enterprise_docs(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, tenant_id uuid NOT NULL, content text NOT NULL, embedding vector(1536) ); CREATE INDEX ON doc_chunks USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops); ALTER TABLE doc_chunks ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON doc_chunks USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid); Retrieval in one query Embed the question with the same model you used for the documents. Then open a transaction and set the tenant for this request. The true at the end of set_config scopes the setting to the transaction, so a pooled connection never carries one customer's tenant into the next request. In the query, <=> is cosine distance: order by it and take the top five. Because it's plain SQL, the chunks join the business data in the same statement: only active documents, only chunks that already have an embedding. No second system, no metadata copy. The last line applies a distance threshold. If nothing is close enough, return nothing. An agent with no context should say "I don't know", not improvise from the fifth-best match. export async Keeping embeddings fresh When a document changes, three things happen in one transaction: the new content is saved, the old chunks are removed, and an outbox event is written. Either all of it commits or none of it does. For a few seconds the document has no chunks, so it simply isn't retrieved. Missing context is safe; stale context is not. The worker does the slow part outside the transaction: split, embed, write back. If the document was deleted in the meantime, there's nothing to do. And the write-back checks the version, so a slow job can never overwrite a newer document with old vectors. await db.transaction(async (tx) => { await tx.query('UPDATE enterprise_docs SET content = $2, updated_at = now() WHERE id = $1', [id, content]); await tx.query('DELETE FROM doc_chunks WHERE doc_id = $1', [id]); await tx.query("INSERT INTO outbox (topic, doc_id) VALUES ('doc.changed', $1)", [id]); }); new Worker('embeddings', async (job) => { // deleted: its chunks went with it await docs.replaceChunks(doc.id, doc.updatedAt, chunks, vectors); // skipped if the doc changed Where this breaks Filtered search. HNSW finds the nearest neighbours first and applies your filter after. With a selective filter, like one small tenant in a huge table, you ask for five results and get two. pgvector 0.8 added iterative index scans for exactly this; turn them on: SET hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order; Index memory. HNSW is fast when the index fits in RAM. Size the instance for it, and expect index builds on millions of rows to take a while. Exact identifiers. Ask for contract C-4471 and vector search returns contracts that look similar. Embeddings are bad at codes and SKUs. Postgres already has full-text search, so combine both rankings in one query. Real scale. For most companies, with thousands to tens of millions of chunks, Postgres is enough. At billions of vectors or thousands of queries per second, a dedicated vector database earns its cost. Choose it for that reason, not by default. What the business gets One system of record for data and embeddings: one backup, one audit trail, and one access model your security team has already reviewed. No sync job, so no orphaned vectors and no agent quoting deleted documents. One query per question instead of two round trips, and one less vendor to contract, secure and monitor. You don't need a new database to build RAG. You need the one you already have, used properly. The numbers in the video are targets for an illustrative scenario, not measurements. The code here is simplified; the full version is in the repository. ▶️ Watch the video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HlT40sMLex0 💻 Full code: https://github.com/NodeNeuralAI/examples/tree/main/v2-rag-pgvector 🔔 More enterprise AI architecture every week: https://www.youtube.com/@NodeNeuralAI?sub_confirmation=1

articles.title: DotShare Part 2: Review, receipts, and an encrypted publishing library
articles.description: In Part 1, a post started in Codex, passed through a saved preview in VS Code, and ended with a public Mastodon receipt. The engineering work behind that flow came down to three questions. What exactly did I approve? What happens if the process dies during delivery? Where do drafts and credentials live? I wanted those answers to survive a restart. DotShare 3.6.0 and CLI 3.0.0 ship the same publishing library across the VS Code interface, CLI, and local MCP server. The library stores drafts, their revisions, and publication attempts. The platform adapter reports what it actually delivered. Release and changelog. A preview belongs to a specific revision create_draft returns a saved draft ID and revision. update_draft checks the expected revision before saving an edit. That matters when I have the library open in VS Code while an agent edits the same record. If one edit wins, the other client needs to reload before saving against the new revision. preview_draft validates the saved revision and creates a preview ID. The preview records the account plan, including the effective copy, thread parts, and media. Before publishing, DotShare revalidates the plan and the local image fingerprints. A change to the draft, an account binding, or the image bytes can require a fresh preview. To publish a saved preview from the CLI, use the draft ID and the revision and preview ID returned by drafts preview. Give that action one stable request ID. dotshare-agent drafts publish DRAFT_ID \ --revision 1 \ --preview-id PREVIEW_ID \ --request-id reviewed-release-1 1 is an example revision. Use the revision you actually reviewed. This command can publish to real accounts, so run it after checking the saved preview and its destinations. Saved draft commands. Templates follow a similar versioning rule. The tool checks which template revision you filled, substitutes literal values, then creates an independent draft with its source template recorded. Effective content is resolved in this order: account override, platform version, shared copy. A preview always uses the resolved version for each selected destination. A retry starts with the receipt journal DotShare reserves a publication operation before sending requests. It records delivery results and receipts per account, including receipts for individual parts of a thread. Repeating the same request ID lets the caller recover that operation instead of sending a second copy. The hard case is a connection drop after a platform accepted the post but before DotShare could confirm it. That case can land in NeedsReview. I inspect the journal and the destination before deciding what to do next. For a multi-account publish, the journal can show which destinations already received their posts. dotshare-agent operation reviewed-release-1 Published records a completed publication. When Dev.to accepts an article sent with published: false, DotShare records SavedRemotely and returns the unpublished article’s receipt. Publication states and recovery. Keep the key and the encrypted records separate The CLI keeps platform tokens in the OS credential store. Linux requires Secret Service. The draft store uses a separate, randomly generated master key, also held in the OS keyring. DotShare uses AES-256-GCM to encrypt the contents of saved drafts, custom templates, and operation journals. Authentication ties each encrypted record to its identity, so a swapped or modified record fails verification. This protects the shared library records on disk. Account labels and other non-secret metadata use private files. The OS credential provider, original images, VS Code’s separate composer drafts, and data held by DotSuite’s cloud backend have their own storage rules. Local security model. I also removed the legacy CLI route that forwarded platform credentials through a relay. The new CLI publishes directly through named accounts. Local image uploads are limited to directories explicitly configured for the MCP server. DotSuite cloud scheduling uses a separate set of connected accounts. CLI upgrade notes. Upgrade and practice a restore For an existing library, stop active publications, install the current CLI, and run the migration. npm install -g dotshare-cli dotshare-agent security status dotshare-agent security protect protect verifies access to the keyring, fixes local permissions where needed, and encrypts older plaintext records in place. It reads back each migrated record to verify the original content survived. If the MCP launcher path changed, review the replacement configuration with dotshare-agent setup --dry-run --replace. After applying it, restart the MCP clients and VS Code, then run dotshare-agent doctor --check-accounts. For the restore test, I used a disposable library with a draft and a publication receipt. I copied the encrypted files and security.json to a new directory. A missing key and an incorrect key both caused reads to fail. Restoring the matching test key through the OS keyring recovered the draft and the original receipt. That’s the recovery dependency to plan for: keep the encrypted library and its matching keyring backup. Recovery instructions. What I verified before shipping Automated checks. 353 tests passed across 33 suites. The CLI and MCP smoke checks also exercised templates, variants, and saved drafts through the installed package. Upgrade and restore. A legacy test draft and receipt survived encryption and could be read back. Repeating the migration had no additional records to convert. The restore test exercised the actual OS keyring with a disposable key. Live publishing. One real draft went from Codex to the VS Code library to a public Mastodon post. I verified the saved Published status and receipt. Public test post. Distribution. The CLI installed from npm as 3.0.0. The 3.6.0 extension was available from Visual Studio Marketplace, Open VSX, and the GitHub release. The DotSuite product page also gained a Docs tab with both guides. npm · Marketplace · Open VSX · DotSuite docs. If you try the workflow, I’d like to know which part of your own publishing process you’d keep in the editor. Account variants and review steps are especially interesting because teams often handle them differently. DotShare on GitHub. I used AI assistance to draft and edit this write-up. The implementation, release checks, and live test are linked above.
